title: Cypress task exposes arbitrary configuration values
description: The Cypress Node task interface exposes a generic configuration getter to its caller. Any Cypress-side caller can supply an arbitrary configuration path and receive the corresponding value, rather than using an allowlisted set of test-only values. If secrets or internal deployment settings are present in the configuration, a compromised or untrusted test/spec can retrieve them through this task and exfiltrate them. The same broad trust assumption is also visible in the generic memory-property lookup. This is primarily a test-environment security-boundary weakness; exploitability in production depends on who can execute Cypress tests and whether sensitive values are loaded into the configuration.

trace.description: A Cypress-side caller outside this file invokes the registered `GetFromConfig` task and supplies an attacker-controlled configuration variable name.
The task forwards the caller-supplied variable name directly to the application configuration provider without an allowlist or sensitivity check.
`config.get(variable)` returns the selected configuration value to the Cypress caller, allowing retrieval of arbitrary loaded configuration entries.

title: Caller-controlled filename permits traversal outside the static data directory
description: The exported loader accepts a caller-controlled `file` value and constructs a filesystem path by concatenating it with the intended static-data directory before calling `path.resolve`. Because `path.resolve` normalizes traversal segments rather than constraining the result to `./data/static`, a value such as `../../secrets/config` can cause the server to read `secrets/config.yml` outside the static-data directory. The `.yml` suffix limits the exact targets but does not provide authorization or directory confinement, enabling unauthorized disclosure of readable YAML files.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies the exported function's `file` parameter without any visible authorization or allow-list validation.

The caller-controlled value is concatenated into a path and normalized with `path.resolve`; traversal segments such as `../../` can escape `./data/static`. No check verifies that the resolved path remains beneath the intended directory.
The resulting path is passed to `readFile`, allowing the process to disclose any readable file reachable through a traversed `.yml` path.

title: Unbounded address collection retrieval
description: The service exposes an unpaginated collection request to the Address API. Any caller outside this file can invoke `get()`, which issues a request for the entire address collection without a page size, limit, or other client-side bound. If the backing endpoint returns all matching records, a large address table can cause excessive response size, browser memory consumption, server query work, and network usage from a single request. Whether the server independently enforces pagination or a maximum result size is not visible in this file.

trace.description: Caller is outside this file and can invoke the exported service method `get()`; the method accepts no pagination or result-limit parameters.
`get()` constructs a collection request against the configured Address API endpoint without adding pagination, a maximum result count, or a timeout.
`HttpClient.get(this.host)` performs the unbounded collection request, and the response is mapped into memory for the caller.

title: Unbounded buffering of streamed chat responses
description: `streamMessages` accepts an arbitrary number of messages and unbounded message content from its caller, then initiates an HTTP request without any size, count, timeout, or cancellation limit. More importantly, the response subscription continues producing chunks independently of the async-generator consumer, while every parsed response chunk is appended to the in-memory `chunks` array. A caller that does not consume the generator, consumes it slowly, or submits a prompt that causes a very large streamed response can cause the browser to retain an unbounded amount of data, resulting in client-side memory exhaustion or degraded application availability. The backend may also incur unbounded LLM/request cost if it does not impose its own limits.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies an arbitrary `messages` array to the exported `streamMessages` method; this method performs no message-count, content-size, or request-cost validation.
The supplied messages are forwarded directly in the POST body to the chat endpoint, with no client-side payload limit, timeout, or cancellation mechanism.
The HTTP subscription processes every download-progress event and parses each streamed `data:` record, allowing the amount of response data processed to scale with the server response.

Each generated chunk is appended to the unbounded `chunks` array. The subscription can continue receiving and buffering chunks even when the async-generator consumer is absent or slower than the producer, allowing attacker-triggered response volume to accumulate in browser memory.

title: Caller-controlled basket IDs enable potential basket BOLA
description: The service accepts a caller-supplied basket identifier and uses it directly in basket retrieval and mutation requests without any client-side binding to the authenticated user's basket. The same pattern exists in find(), get(), put(), del(), checkout(), and applyCoupon(). If the corresponding server endpoints do not independently enforce ownership, an authenticated user can substitute another user's basket ID to read, modify, delete, check out, or apply coupons to that basket. The sessionStorage value used by updateNumberOfCartItems() is only a client-side identifier and is not an authorization control.

trace.description: The public find(id) method receives the basket identifier from a caller outside this file; the identifier is not derived from a verified server-side identity.

The supplied id is interpolated into the basket URL. No ownership or authorization check is performed in this service before issuing the request; equivalent ID handling is present in get(), put(), del(), checkout(), and applyCoupon().
HttpClient performs the GET request for the selected basket. If backend authorization is absent or insufficient, replacing id with another user's basket ID exposes the other basket's contents.

title: Arbitrary update properties are forwarded to the basket API
description: The generic put() method accepts an arbitrary params object and forwards it wholesale as the update body. There is no explicit allow-list of basket-item properties. A caller who can invoke this service or alter the generated request can supply server-side fields beyond quantity, such as ownership, basket association, product, pricing, or status fields, if the backend binds request properties directly to its model. This is a client-side mass-assignment boundary and requires backend rejection/allow-listing to be safe.

trace.description: The public put(id, params) method receives both the target resource ID and an unrestricted params object from a caller outside this file.
The params object is passed through without validation or an explicit property allow-list. The declared type is any, so the service imposes no field-level boundary.
HttpClient sends the complete caller-supplied object as the PUT request body. If the API performs automatic model binding, unauthorized model properties can be persisted.

title: Unrestricted caller-controlled notification URL
description: The service accepts an arbitrary URL from its caller and forwards it directly to Angular's HttpClient without an allowlist, origin restriction, or scheme validation. If an attacker can influence the URL supplied by a caller elsewhere in the application, they can cause the application to issue requests to attacker-chosen or internal endpoints. Depending on configured HTTP interceptors and browser/server deployment, this may trigger authenticated cross-origin requests, CSRF-like side effects, or retrieval of notification data from an unintended origin. The caller and URL source are outside this file, so reachability cannot be confirmed here.

The caller-supplied URL is passed unchanged to HttpClient, allowing requests to arbitrary destinations selected by the caller.

title: Unbounded retrieval of all hints
description: The service exposes a collection-wide retrieval operation with no pagination, maximum result count, or other client-side bound. A caller outside this file can invoke `getAll()`, causing the application to request and materialize every hint returned by `/api/Hints/` in one response. If the collection grows or is attacker-influenced, a single request can consume excessive server, network, and browser memory resources and degrade availability.

title: Unbounded order-history retrieval without pagination
description: The `getAll()` method issues a request for the entire order collection via `/rest/order-history/orders` without accepting or sending pagination parameters. If the server returns all matching orders, a caller can trigger an unbounded response, causing excessive server query work, network transfer, and frontend memory consumption. The actual caller and any server-side pagination or rate limiting are outside this file, so exploitability depends on the endpoint implementation.

title: Unrestricted payment-card fields forwarded to Cards API
description: The exported `save(params)` method accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied object and forwards it unchanged as the request body to the Cards API. There is no explicit allow-list of card properties in this service, so any fields accepted and persisted by the backend—including potentially server-managed fields such as ownership, verification, or payment metadata—can be supplied by a caller of this method. The backend API is outside the reviewed file, so the impact depends on whether its request-to-model binding also lacks property-level authorization; direct client-side forwarding provides no protection against such fields being submitted.

The arbitrary `params` object is passed unchanged as the POST body; this service performs no explicit field allow-listing or removal of server-managed card properties before crossing the API boundary.

title: Unbounded photo upload passed to the memories endpoint
description: The service accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied File and immediately places it in a multipart upload without enforcing a size or count limit. Because the caller is outside this file, an attacker able to invoke the application or reproduce the request can submit very large images repeatedly, causing server-side memory, disk, bandwidth, or image-processing consumption. No client-side bound is visible here, and server-side enforcement cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: Unpaginated retrieval of the complete photo wall
description: The photo-wall read operation requests the entire memories collection in one response and exposes no pagination, page-size parameter, or client-side result bound. If the collection grows large or an attacker can cause many memories to exist, a single request can force the API and browser to transfer and materialize an unbounded result set, consuming server and client memory and bandwidth. A server-side cap is not visible from this file.

title: Unbounded product review retrieval
description: The service exposes a public `get` operation that retrieves a product's complete review collection in one HTTP request. The request contains no page number, page size, or other bound, and the response is materialized and returned to the caller. If the backend endpoint returns all reviews for the product, a product with a very large review history can cause excessive response size, client memory use, and server/database work from a single request. Pagination or a server-enforced result cap is not represented here.

The method constructs a reviews collection request using only the product identifier. No pagination parameters, maximum result count, timeout, or client-side bound is supplied.
`HttpClient.get` performs the collection retrieval, and the response's `data` collection is passed through without limiting its size.

title: Unbounded fetch of the entire quantity collection
description: The service exposes an unbounded fetch-all operation. A caller outside this file can invoke `getAll()`, which issues a request for the complete `Quantitys` collection without pagination, a maximum result count, or any client-side response bound. If the corresponding API returns a large or attacker-influenced collection, one request can allocate substantial browser memory and transfer bandwidth, potentially degrading the client and API. Server-side limits may mitigate this, but they are not visible here.

The method constructs a collection request ending in `/api/Quantitys/` and maps the entire response data set, with no pagination, maximum count, timeout, or response-size control.

title: Unbounded recycle collection query
description: The public `find` method accepts arbitrary caller-supplied query parameters and forwards them directly to the recycle collection endpoint without enforcing pagination, a maximum page size, or another result bound. A caller can invoke the collection request with parameters that cause the server to return a very large recycle dataset (subject to backend behavior), consuming server memory, bandwidth, and client resources. No compensating limit is visible in this service; backend-side limits cannot be confirmed from this file.

The supplied parameters are forwarded unchanged as the HTTP query parameter object, with no pagination or maximum-result enforcement.

The service issues a collection GET request to `/api/Recycles/`; if the backend honors broad or large result queries, one caller-triggered request can return an unbounded result set and consume server, network, and client resources.

title: Unbounded local backup read and JSON parsing can exhaust browser resources
description: The exported restore() method accepts an attacker-controlled File and reads the entire file into memory before parsing it, with no maximum file-size or content-length check. A sufficiently large or deeply nested JSON backup can cause substantial browser memory consumption, UI thread blocking, or tab termination when the victim imports it. The caller/file-selection flow is outside this file, but the unbounded read and parse are visible here.

The entire File is converted to text in one operation, with no size limit or streaming/bounded read.
The complete attacker-supplied string is passed to JSON.parse, requiring another large in-memory representation and potentially expensive parsing of deeply nested data.
JSON.parse is the resource-intensive sink: an oversized or pathological backup can block the browser main thread or exhaust tab memory before the promise rejection handler can run.

title: Client-controlled X-User-Email header can enable identity spoofing
description: The interceptor copies a browser-controlled `localStorage` value into the `X-User-Email` request header. Any script running in the origin, browser extension, or user-controlled client can set this value to an arbitrary email, and the server cannot treat it as a trustworthy identity assertion. If any backend route uses `X-User-Email` for authentication, ownership, or authorization decisions instead of deriving the identity from the verified bearer token, an attacker can impersonate another account by setting the stored email before issuing a request. The server should ignore this header for identity decisions and derive the user from the validated token/session.

trace.description: The Angular HTTP interceptor receives each outgoing `HttpRequest`; the caller and attacker-facing request source are outside this file.
The interceptor reads the `email` value directly from browser `localStorage` without cryptographic verification, binding it to the outgoing request based solely on client state.

The unverified value is emitted as `X-User-Email`. A backend that trusts this header can be supplied an attacker-selected identity, permitting account impersonation or bypass of identity-based authorization.

title: MFA temporary token is read from script-accessible localStorage
description: The MFA verification flow reads the temporary authentication token from browser `localStorage` and sends it as a bearer-like credential alongside the TOTP value. Any JavaScript executing in the application's origin, including an XSS payload or compromised third-party script, can read `totp_tmp_token` and potentially use it to complete MFA verification. This file provides no indication that the token is bound to a browser session, protected from script access, or otherwise constrained beyond the server-side endpoint. Authentication material should preferably be held in an HttpOnly, appropriately scoped cookie or another mechanism inaccessible to arbitrary page scripts.

trace.description: The exported `verify` method receives a TOTP token from a caller outside this file and begins the MFA verification request.

The method retrieves `totp_tmp_token` from browser localStorage. This storage is readable by any JavaScript running in the application's origin, so compromise of the frontend origin can expose the temporary authentication credential.

The retrieved temporary token and caller-supplied TOTP token are submitted to the `/rest/2fa/verify` authentication endpoint; possession of the exposed temporary token can assist an attacker in completing the MFA flow.

title: Unbounded selectedLines payload sent to verdict endpoint
description: The public `check` method accepts an arbitrarily large `selectedLines` array and places it directly into an HTTP request body without any client-side size or count limit. A caller outside this file can invoke the method with millions of entries, causing excessive browser memory use during serialization and generating an oversized request that consumes server parsing, bandwidth, and processing resources. Backend request-size limits or rate limiting may mitigate the impact, but no bound is enforced in this service.

trace.description: The exported `check` method receives `selectedLines` from a caller outside this file, with no validation of its length or contents.
The caller-controlled `key` and `selectedLines` values are copied directly into the POST request body.
The unbounded request is issued through `HttpClient`, allowing an attacker-controlled caller to trigger oversized serialization and network/server request-processing costs.

title: Passwords transmitted in URL query parameters
description: The password-change flow places the current password and new password directly in an HTTP GET query string. Query strings are commonly retained in browser history, proxy/load-balancer logs, web-server access logs, monitoring systems, and potentially referrer data. An attacker who obtains any of these records can recover the plaintext credentials and use the new password or reuse the current password against other services. The service does not encode the values into a request body or otherwise prevent URL-based disclosure.

trace.description: The exported changePassword method receives current, new, and repeat password values from a caller outside this file.
The password values are concatenated directly into a URL query string without any protection against URL-based disclosure.

HttpClient issues a GET request containing the plaintext passwords in the request URL; those values can be captured by browser history, intermediary and server access logs, monitoring, or referrer handling.

title: OAuth access token exposed in URL
description: oauthLogin sends a caller-provided OAuth access token as a URL query parameter to the Google userinfo endpoint. URL-based tokens can leak through browser history, proxy and web-server logs, monitoring systems, and Referer headers. Anyone obtaining the token may be able to query the associated account's OAuth user information until the token expires or is revoked.

The access token is concatenated into the fixed Google userinfo URL as the access_token query parameter.
HttpClient performs the outbound request with the bearer credential in the URL, exposing it to URL history, intermediary/server logs, monitoring, and possible referrer leakage.

title: Stored client-side XSS through trusted feedback HTML
description: Feedback comments received from the feedback service are embedded directly into an HTML string and then passed to Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, explicitly disabling Angular's contextual HTML sanitization. An attacker who can submit or otherwise control a feedback comment can inject HTML, including event-handler payloads such as an `` or other executable markup, which is subsequently supplied to the gallery for rendering. No sanitization or allowlisting is applied before the trust bypass.

Each feedback comment is interpolated into a new HTML document fragment containing a `

The constructed HTML, including the untrusted comment, is passed to `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, an explicit Angular security bypass. This marks the attacker-controlled HTML as trusted instead of sanitizing it before gallery rendering.

title: Test configuration disables HTML sanitization

This disables the sanitizer in the test environment, so feedback comments containing HTML or script payloads are passed through as trusted HTML and the test does not verify production sanitization behavior. This is test-only and does not itself prove a production XSS, but it weakens security regression coverage for the component's HTML-rendering path.

The test configures the component's DomSanitizer dependency with a custom mock provider.
The mock implementation of bypassSecurityTrustHtml returns the supplied value unchanged, explicitly disabling sanitization before the component's feedback HTML is processed.

title: Unbounded loading of complete order history
description: The accounting view retrieves the complete order history with `getAll()` and then materializes every returned order into an in-memory array before attaching a paginator. The paginator is client-side and does not bound the server response or the amount of data held in browser memory. As order history grows, a single authenticated visit can force retrieval, JSON parsing, array allocation, and table-model construction for an unbounded number of records, enabling memory and processing exhaustion. No page size, server-side pagination, or other bound is visible in this component.

`loadOrders` calls the order-history service's `getAll()` operation, whose name and invocation provide no visible pagination or bounded query parameters.
Every returned order is copied into `orderData`, causing the response size to translate directly into client-side memory and processing cost.
The full array is passed to `MatTableDataSource`; attaching `MatPaginator` only paginates the already-loaded data and does not constrain the fetch.

title: Client-controlled accounting values lack bounded business validation
description: The component accepts caller-controlled price and quantity values and forwards them to update services after only a lower-bound clamp. There is no upper bound, finite-number check, precision validation, or server-derived validation visible here. A caller able to invoke the component handlers or alter the client request can submit extreme or otherwise invalid positive values; if the corresponding API trusts these values, inventory quantities or product prices can be corrupted, creating an economic and data-integrity impact. Server-side validation is not visible in this file, so exploitability depends on the service endpoints.

The unbounded value is sent directly to the quantity update service as the persisted quantity.
Similarly, `modifyPrice` receives an externally influenced value and applies only the same lower-bound clamp.
The resulting arbitrary price is forwarded directly to the product update service, with no visible maximum, numeric-format, or business-rule validation.

title: Client-controlled address ID used for read and update without ownership enforcement
description: The edit workflow accepts an arbitrary `addressId` from the client-controlled route and uses it to retrieve and update an address without any visible ownership or authorization binding. A user can potentially replace their own route identifier with another user's address ID, causing this component to load and submit changes for that record. The backend may enforce authorization, but no such control is present in this file and the client provides no protection against direct ID substitution.

When saving in edit mode, the same unverified identifier is passed to the update operation. Substituting another user's address ID in the route can therefore target that address if the backend endpoint does not independently enforce ownership.

It does not require a structurally valid JWT, signature verification, or expiration validation. Because this assertion can pass while the guard only checks token presence, it can allow an implementation that accepts attacker-controlled or forged tokens to remain unnoticed. Because the token is stored in localStorage and is browser-modifiable, an attacker can construct a token whose payload contains `data.role` equal to the required role, causing the corresponding guard to permit the route. This is a cryptographic/authentication failure; backend authorization must not rely on this client-side decision.

The route definitions also accept attacker-controlled identifiers such as :id and :entity without any route-level identity binding.

title: Token sale access relies on an obfuscated client-side URL secret
description: The token-sale route is protected only by a client-side, obfuscated constant embedded in the JavaScript bundle. tokenMatcher reconstructs the expected path from hardcoded arithmetic and string operations, then routes the request to TokenSaleComponent when it matches. Anyone who can download the frontend bundle can reverse this value or observe it during execution, so the route cannot serve as a trustworthy authorization mechanism. If the token-sale component exposes any privileged or valuable operation, the hidden path is discoverable and bypasses any intended secrecy. Server-side authorization would be required for protection.

The matcher derives a fixed token string from hardcoded numeric arguments and compares the first URL segment against it. The value is present in recoverable form in the client bundle rather than being obtained from a trusted server-side authorization decision.
A matching client-controlled path activates TokenSaleComponent. No authentication, role check, or server-backed authorization guard is attached to this route.

title: Unbounded socket notifications enable client resource exhaustion
description: The component accepts every socket-delivered `challenge solved` message and appends a notification to an unbounded in-memory array. There is no maximum notification count, eviction policy, rate limiting, or cancellation of pending translation operations. A caller who can cause repeated challenge-solved events—or a compromised/misbehaving socket peer—can grow `notifications` indefinitely, trigger repeated change detection and DOM work, and consume browser memory. Each non-restore event also invokes `saveProgress()`, creating an additional unbounded sequence of progress requests and cookie writes.

The handler processes each message without any frequency, count, or payload-size limit, and invokes notification handling for every non-hidden event.
Each accepted event is passed to `showNotification`, while non-restore events also trigger `saveProgress`, allowing repeated events to create repeated downstream work.
`showNotification` asynchronously processes each event and constructs a notification from attacker-influenced socket fields such as `challenge`, `key`, and `flag`.
Every processed event is appended to `this.notifications`; the array has no size bound or automatic eviction, and change detection is forced after each append.
On the separate non-restore path, each event also calls the progress service without a local rate or concurrency limit, amplifying network and client work.

title: Privileged password policy failure does not block password change
description: The component treats the privileged-account password policy as a warning rather than an enforcement control. When the locally stored email matches `support@.*`, a password failing the 12-character complexity expression only triggers `console.error`; execution continues directly into `userService.changePassword()`. An attacker can alter `localStorage.email` or invoke the method with a weak password, and the client still submits the password-change request. If the backend relies on this client-side policy, the privileged-account password requirement is bypassed, weakening account protection.

The privileged-account determination is based on attacker-modifiable browser `localStorage`, and a failed complexity check only emits a browser-console warning. There is no return, validation failure, or other state transition preventing submission.
The component unconditionally invokes the password-change service after the warning, passing the attacker-selected current, new, and repeated passwords.

title: Password-change form permits five-character passwords
description: The new-password control is configured with a minimum length of only five characters. This is a weak password-policy setting for a password-change flow, and the component does not apply the stronger 12-character complexity policy to ordinary accounts. If this client-side policy is reflected or trusted by the backend, users can select short, easily guessable passwords, increasing the likelihood of account takeover. The finding is limited to the unsafe configuration visible here; backend enforcement cannot be confirmed from this file.

The configured value is used in the password-change request sent through `UserService`, allowing a five-character value to reach the change-password operation when accepted by the surrounding form flow.

title: Unbounded chat input, response streaming, and conversation growth
description: The component accepts message content from callers outside this file, including the attacker-controllable `initialMessage` query parameter, and forwards it to the chat service without any length, token, or conversation-size limit. The response stream is also consumed until the service ends it, while each `deltaContent` and tool-call chunk is appended to the in-memory message object. A caller can submit an extremely large message or trigger an unbounded/very large model response, causing client memory growth and potentially excessive LLM/API expenditure. The full accumulated conversation is sent on every subsequent request, further multiplying resource use.

The content is added to the conversation without a maximum length or token limit, and the entire accumulated message history is prepared for the API on every request.
The unbounded conversation is submitted to the chat service, and the asynchronous stream is consumed without a timeout, maximum chunk count, maximum output size, or cancellation limit.

title: Raw configuration errors exposed through console logging
description: The configuration request's raw error object is written directly to the browser console. Because the error originates from an external configuration/service call, it may contain backend URLs, response details, stack information, or other diagnostic data. Browser-console logging is visible to the user and does not provide structured, centralized security monitoring; in production it can expose internal details while still failing to create an auditable event for incident response.

title: Continuation bearer code stored in a long-lived, insufficiently protected cookie
description: The helper stores the server-issued continuation code in a browser cookie with a one-year lifetime, while supplying only an expiration option. No Secure or SameSite protections are configured, and a client-side cookie API cannot provide HttpOnly protection. If this continuation code acts as a bearer token for advancing the coding-challenge workflow, it can be exposed through plaintext HTTP, cross-site cookie transmission, or JavaScript-accessible storage, and remains usable for an unnecessarily long period after theft. The caller and server-side validation are outside this file, so the token's exact privileges cannot be confirmed here.

title: Client-supplied user identity and rating are submitted as trusted feedback properties
description: The component constructs the feedback request using client-controlled identity and business-significant fields. In particular, it copies the client-side UserId control value and rating into the object sent to the feedback service. A caller who modifies the Angular state or intercepts/replays the request can substitute another user ID or alter the rating. The server must derive the author from the authenticated session and independently validate the rating; that server-side enforcement is outside this file and cannot be confirmed here.

These are caller-modifiable request properties rather than values that can be trusted as authorization or authorship decisions.

title: Client-controlled complaint UserId can be spoofed
description: The component places the authenticated user's identifier into a mutable complaint object and sends that object to the complaint API. Because `UserId` is supplied as part of the client-generated request rather than being derived and enforced server-side, a caller can modify the object or intercept the request before submission and replace `UserId` with another user's identifier. If the API persists the submitted property, this allows complaint attribution or ownership to be spoofed and represents a sensitive property crossing the client/API boundary without an explicit allow-list or server-side authority check. The server-side handling is outside this file, so whether the backend accepts the forged field cannot be confirmed here.

title: Unbounded system notification polling frequency can cause request storms
description: The notification polling interval is taken directly from application configuration and only checked for truthiness. Negative values and extremely small positive values are accepted. A negative interval is effectively scheduled as an immediate/zero-delay interval by RxJS, while a very small positive interval can create a request storm through repeated calls to `fetchNotification`. If the configuration is attacker-influenced or deployed with an unsafe value, this can consume browser and notification-service resources and degrade availability. The caller supplying the configuration is outside this file.

Each interval can initiate a notification fetch, allowing an unsafe interval to generate excessive repeated requests.

title: Browser-controlled address ID is fetched without visible ownership enforcement
description: The component reads the address identifier directly from browser-controlled sessionStorage and passes it to the address lookup service without any ownership or authorization check in this code. A user can modify sessionStorage (for example, using browser developer tools) to replace addressId with another address identifier, causing the component to request that address. If the corresponding backend lookup is not independently scoped to the authenticated user, this enables a BOLA-style disclosure of another user's address. The frontend must not be treated as an authorization boundary, and this flow provides no visible per-resource authorization control.

No per-user ownership or authorization check is present between identifier selection and response handling; exploitation depends on the backend service also lacking that check.

title: Untrusted CAPTCHA HTML explicitly marked as trusted
description: The CAPTCHA response field `data.image` is received from an external service and passed directly to Angular's `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, disabling Angular's HTML sanitization. If the CAPTCHA service response can be influenced, compromised, or manipulated by an attacker, HTML/SVG payloads in the image content will be treated as trusted markup and rendered by the component. title: Exported API data reaches an unsanitized document.write XSS sink
description: The data-export response's `userData` is written with `document.write`, which parses the value as HTML in a newly opened browser window. The value comes from an external API response and is not escaped or sanitized in this component. If exported data contains attacker-controlled stored content, such as a malicious profile or other persisted field, opening the export executes HTML/script-capable payloads in the application's browser origin. The new-window boundary does not make `document.write` safe because the document is created by the application and receives raw markup.

title: Unredacted configuration errors exposed through browser console logging
description: The configuration-loading error handler writes the complete error object to the browser console. Because this object originates from the configuration request, it may contain backend error details, request metadata, URLs, or stack traces that are exposed to any user who can open developer tools. This weakens confidentiality of diagnostic information and provides no controlled, redacted security logging path for investigating configuration-service failures.

The external configuration response is processed and may supply application metadata, establishing that failures in this remote request are handled by this component.

title: Challenge prerequisite enforced only by client-side UI state
description: The component treats the disabled mint button as the enforcement mechanism for the challenge prerequisite, but `mintNFT()` itself checks only whether a wallet session exists. A caller can invoke the public method directly from browser JavaScript or otherwise bypass the UI, approve 1000 BEE, and call `mintNFT()` without `challengeSolved` being true. The later `verifyNFTWallet()` call records the result after minting rather than preventing the unauthorized mint. If the NFT contract does not independently enforce the challenge requirement, this permits bypassing the intended challenge workflow and potentially minting NFTs without satisfying it.

After only checking `session`, the method submits the approval and then invokes the NFT contract's `mintNFT()` operation, allowing direct callers to skip the UI gate.

title: Unbounded user-controlled faucet withdrawal amount
description: `extractBEETokens()` forwards the caller-supplied withdrawal amount directly to the faucet contract without a client-side maximum, positivity check, or other business-rule validation. The value defaults from the component's externally bindable `withdrawAmount` field and can also be supplied directly as the method argument. If the faucet contract does not independently enforce a per-withdrawal/per-user cap, an attacker can request an excessive amount and potentially drain faucet funds; even when the contract rejects invalid values, malformed or extreme inputs can cause repeated failed transactions and user-funded gas consumption.

title: Password-recovery flow exposes account existence and security questions
description: The password-recovery flow lets an unauthenticated user submit arbitrary email values to `findBy` and then exposes whether an account exists and, when it does, the account's security question. The distinct branches enable account enumeration, while returning the security question gives an attacker information useful for targeting the password-reset challenge. The component applies only client-side email validation and does not provide an application-level privacy-preserving response.

title: Password-recovery lookup lacks an observable rate-limit control

Although `clearTimeout` debounces ordinary typing, a caller can repeatedly change the email value and cause a new `findBy` request roughly every `timeoutDuration` interval. If the backing endpoint performs database lookups or reveals account state, repeated requests can be used for request amplification, enumeration, or service degradation. No server-side rate limit is visible in this file, so the finding is conditional on the service/API not enforcing one elsewhere.

title: Untrusted JWT claim reaches Angular HTML sanitization bypass
description: The component reads a JWT from attacker-modifiable browser storage, decodes it without verification, and uses the `data.lastLoginIp` claim as HTML after explicitly disabling Angular's sanitization. The unverified decoding also means the client accepts arbitrary claim contents from a forged or modified local-storage token.

title: Hardcoded testing account credentials exposed in frontend source
description: The login component ships a plaintext testing account username and password in the frontend bundle. Because this code is delivered to every browser, any visitor can recover the credentials and authenticate as the test account. If the account remains enabled in a deployed environment, this is a hardcoded/default credential exposure.

title: Authentication token stored in script-accessible storage and cookie without transport protections

Persisting the token in localStorage also makes it readable by any script executing in the origin. title: Client-side accounting authorization trusts a decoded localStorage token

A caller can replace or modify the localStorage token to make the UI treat the session as accounting. If the navbar exposes accounting-only navigation or actions based on this method, those controls can be reached without a trustworthy server-side role decision. title: OAuth users receive predictable Base64-encoded email passwords

If the production component follows the behavior asserted by this test, an attacker can authenticate to the newly created regular account through the normal login flow without learning a user-chosen secret. The exact implementation is outside this test file, but the test explicitly establishes the insecure credential-generation contract.

The OAuth initialization path processes the response and triggers account provisioning using the email-derived credential.

title: Unsupported payment mode bypasses deluxe membership payment
