title: SQL injection in login query enables authentication bypass
description: The unauthenticated POST /rest/user/login handler interpolates the caller-controlled email directly into a raw SQL statement. An attacker can submit an email value containing SQL syntax, such as a quote followed by an always-true predicate and a comment, altering the WHERE clause and potentially bypassing password authentication or changing the selected user. The password value is also embedded into the SQL string, although the directly controllable email field is sufficient for exploitation.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/login reaches the exported login handler; the route has no authentication middleware, and the caller is outside this file. Request data is received through req.body.
The attacker-controlled req.body.email value is inserted into a template literal. The password hash is likewise inserted into the SQL text rather than passed as a bound parameter.
sequelize.query executes the assembled SQL statement with no parameter bindings or allow-listing. User input therefore changes SQL parsing rather than being treated solely as data.

title: Login endpoint has no visible rate limiting or brute-force protection
description: The public login endpoint performs a database authentication query for every request without any visible per-IP, per-account, or per-endpoint throttling, attempt counter, or backoff. An attacker can repeatedly submit login requests to consume database and application resources while also conducting password or credential-stuffing attacks. Infrastructure-level rate limiting cannot be confirmed from this file, so the finding is based on the missing control in the route implementation.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/login is publicly reachable with auth: none; the route registration is outside this file, and the exported handler receives each attacker request here.
Every invocation immediately runs verifyPreLoginChallenges (which is empty) and proceeds to authentication without a rate-limit, lockout, delay, or request-count check.
Each request reaches the database query, allowing an unbounded caller to repeatedly consume database connections and query capacity.

title: Authentication successes and failures are not logged
description: This login flow contains no security-event logging for failed authentication attempts or successful logins. Both invalid credentials and successful authentication produce responses without recording the account identifier, outcome, source context, or timestamp in this file. If no centralized middleware logs these events, attackers can perform credential attacks without an auditable trail and operators cannot reliably detect or investigate them.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/login is the attacker-facing authentication entrypoint; the caller and any external logging middleware are outside this file.
The handler evaluates the authentication result and branches to either the successful login flow or an invalid-credentials response, but no logger or audit event is invoked on either path.
The failed-login path directly returns a 401 response, while the successful path directly creates and returns a token, with no security-relevant event being recorded in this handler.

title: Race condition allows duplicate likes and inflated like counts
description: The handler attempts to enforce one like per user with a read/check followed by separate updates, but the sequence is not atomic. Two concurrent requests from the same authenticated user can both read a review without that user's email in `likedBy`, both increment `likesCount`, and then append the email. This can create duplicate entries and inflate the like count beyond the intended one-like-per-user invariant. The artificial delay at line 41 makes the race window substantially easier to exploit.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported middleware receives the attacker-controlled request; the route caller and HTTP registration are outside this file. The route is POST /rest/products/reviews and authentication middleware is applied externally.
The target review identifier is taken directly from the request body, and the review is loaded by that identifier.
The handler checks whether the authenticated user's email is already present, but this check is performed independently of the subsequent writes.
The like counter is incremented in a separate database operation after the check, allowing concurrent requests to each increment the counter.
An artificial 150 ms delay expands the interval during which another request can pass the same check.
The handler rereads the review and appends the authenticated user's email to the in-memory array without rechecking or enforcing uniqueness.
The modified array is written back with a separate update, so concurrent requests can persist duplicate user entries and leave `likedBy` inconsistent with `likesCount`.

title: Unthrottled review-like endpoint with artificial request delay
description: This authenticated write endpoint has no visible per-user, per-IP, or per-route rate limit. Each request performs multiple database operations and deliberately waits 150 ms before the second read/write phase. An attacker with a valid account can send many concurrent requests to keep request and database resources occupied and amplify the race condition. Reverse-proxy or global rate limiting may mitigate this, but no such control is present in this file.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported handler receives POST requests from outside this file. The route is protected only by authentication; no rate-limiting middleware is shown for this handler.
Each request performs a review lookup and then database updates, with no request-count or concurrency limit in the handler.
The deliberate 150 ms asynchronous wait keeps each request active before additional database work, allowing a caller to consume request and connection capacity through concurrent submissions.

title: Unbounded public memory listing enables resource exhaustion
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/memories handler retrieves every memory record in a single request with an eager UserModel association and returns the complete result set. There is no pagination, maximum result count, or other application-level bound. As the number of memories grows, an attacker can repeatedly request this public endpoint to force increasingly large database results, joins, serialization, and response buffering, potentially exhausting application memory or database capacity and causing denial of service.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported handler receives requests for the unauthenticated GET /rest/memories route; the route caller and its lack of authentication are outside this file.
The handler performs an unbounded findAll operation over all memories and eagerly loads the associated UserModel records. No limit, pagination, timeout, or caller-based throttling is applied.

title: Unbounded retrieval and in-memory reversal of all orders
description: The accounting order-history endpoint retrieves the entire orders collection with no pagination, limit, date range, or other caller-controlled bound. The result is then reversed in memory before being serialized. A caller with accounting access can repeatedly invoke this endpoint and force the database, application memory, CPU, and response bandwidth to scale with the total number of orders, potentially degrading service or causing an outage as the collection grows.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an external HTTP request from the caller outside this file for GET /rest/order-history/orders; route-level protection requires accounting access.
The handler issues an unbounded collection query with no pagination, limit, timeout, or other result-size restriction.

The complete result set is reversed in application memory and returned as a JSON response, causing memory, CPU, serialization, and bandwidth consumption proportional to the total number of stored orders.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of internal application metrics
description: The unauthenticated GET /metrics route exposes the Prometheus registry directly. The registry includes aggregate wallet balance, user counts, order/review/complaint counts, challenge progress, and cheat-score information. Because the route has no authentication or authorization middleware, any remote caller can retrieve internal operational and potentially sensitive business metrics.

trace.description: The exported metrics handler receives an attacker-controlled request; the caller and route registration are outside this file, and the provided route mapping registers GET /metrics without authentication.
The handler prepares a response using the Prometheus content type and the global registry, which contains application metrics populated by observeMetrics().

The complete registry is serialized and returned to the requester without an authorization check or filtering. The registry includes metrics such as total wallet balance, registered-user counts, order counts, complaint counts, and cheat-score data.

title: Unbounded Prometheus label cardinality from upload MIME types
description: The file-upload metrics middleware uses the client-supplied multipart MIME type as an unrestricted Prometheus label value. Prometheus client label children are retained in the registry, so an attacker can submit repeated uploads with distinct MIME types (or otherwise vary the client-provided MIME value) to create unbounded time-series entries. This can grow process and registry memory and increase the cost of /metrics scrapes. The middleware runs before the route's later file-type validation, so that validation does not constrain the label cardinality at this point.

trace.description: The exported upload-observation middleware receives requests containing uploaded files; its caller and the unauthenticated upload routes are outside this file, including /file-upload and /profile/image/file.

For every completed response, the middleware takes the uploaded file's MIME type and uses it as the file_type metric label. The value originates from the client-controlled multipart upload metadata and is not allow-listed or bounded here.

The code increments a Prometheus Counter child selected by the attacker-controlled MIME type. Each distinct label value can create and retain another time series, allowing repeated requests with unique values to consume process memory and inflate metric scrape size.

title: Unauthenticated access to premium content
description: The premium-content handler is reachable through the externally registered GET route without authentication or authorization middleware, and the handler performs no payment, entitlement, or role check before serving the private asset. Any unauthenticated caller who knows or discovers the route can retrieve the supposedly paywalled content directly.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the externally registered GET /this/page/is/hidden/behind/an/incredibly/high/paywall/that/could/only/be/unlocked/by/sending/1btc/to/us route invokes this exported handler with no authentication middleware; the caller and route registration are outside this file.
The handler ignores the request identity and any payment or entitlement state, then sends the private premium wallpaper to every caller without an authorization check.

title: Unbounded payment-card listing can consume application resources
description: The authenticated GET /api/Cards handler retrieves every payment card belonging to the authenticated user with an unbounded CardModel.findAll call. There is no pagination, maximum result count, or other per-request bound. If a user accumulates or causes a large number of cards to exist, one request can load and transform the entire collection in memory, and repeated requests can consume database, CPU, and application memory resources. The query is user-scoped, so this is a resource-consumption issue rather than an access-control issue.

trace.description: The caller outside this file reaches the exported handler registered as GET /api/Cards; the route has authentication middleware, but this handler accepts the request and performs the collection operation.
The handler queries all cards for the user via CardModel.findAll without a limit, offset, cursor, or page-size constraint. The result size is therefore not bounded by this request handler.

Each returned card is iterated and transformed into a response object, with all transformed cards retained in displayableCards and returned in a single JSON response. This creates memory and response-work proportional to the user's total card count.

title: NFT verification accepts an unsigned, caller-controlled wallet identity
description: The wallet verification handler accepts a caller-supplied wallet address as proof of wallet ownership. It only checks whether that string is present in the process-wide set of addresses that emitted an NFT mint event, then marks the challenge solved. No wallet signature, transaction authorization, or other cryptographic proof demonstrates that the caller controls the address. Because blockchain mint events and wallet addresses are observable, an attacker can submit another user's recently minted address and consume the one-time verification entry, potentially solving the challenge without controlling that wallet.

trace.description: The exported wallet verification handler receives an external HTTP request; its route is registered as unauthenticated for POST /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify. The caller is outside this file.
The handler copies the caller-controlled request body field walletAddress into metamaskAddress without validating ownership or requiring a signature.

The caller-controlled address is treated as an authenticated identity solely because it matches an address in the minted-address set; on a match, the server deletes the entry and returns success with the challenge status. There is no cryptographic proof that the caller controls the wallet.

title: Unauthenticated NFT listener initialization is raceable and unbounded
description: The unauthenticated listener-initialization endpoint has a race in its singleton guard. isEventListenerCreated is checked before asynchronous module import and WebSocket provider setup complete, but is set to true only afterward. Multiple concurrent requests can therefore all observe false and each create an Alchemy WebSocket connection and contract event listener. The endpoint has no visible authentication or rate limiting, allowing an attacker to amplify external connections and event-processing work and potentially exhaust sockets or provider quotas.

trace.description: The exported listener handler receives an external HTTP request; it is registered as unauthenticated for GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen. The caller is outside this file.
Each request checks the shared boolean before any asynchronous initialization has completed. Concurrent requests can all observe isEventListenerCreated as false.
Each racing request can create a new WebSocketProvider using the external Alchemy endpoint, consuming a WebSocket connection and provider resources.

Each resulting contract instance registers an NFTMinted event listener. The guard is not set until after this asynchronous work, so concurrent unauthenticated calls can multiply listeners and event-processing load.

title: NFT mint listener retains an unbounded set of minter addresses
description: The process-wide addressesMinted Set has no capacity bound, expiration, or cleanup except when a caller successfully verifies an address. Every distinct minter observed by the long-lived blockchain listener is retained in memory. An attacker able to generate many NFT mint events or wallets can cause unbounded Set growth, eventually increasing memory usage and causing process degradation or termination.

trace.description: The NFTMinted callback receives externally generated blockchain event data; the event source and any caller causing those events are outside this file.
For every distinct minter address, the callback checks the process-wide Set and adds the address when it is not already present. No maximum size, expiration, or periodic cleanup is enforced.

The attacker-influenced address is permanently retained in addressesMinted until a verification request happens to delete it, creating unbounded process memory consumption over the listener's lifetime.

title: Unauthenticated basket checkout enables BOLA and destructive actions
description: The checkout handler is reachable through POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout without authentication middleware. It looks up the basket using only the caller-supplied path identifier and never verifies that the basket belongs to the authenticated caller. The handler then processes the basket and destroys its items, allowing an attacker to substitute another user's basket ID, trigger checkout, consume inventory, and modify the victim's basket.

trace.description: The exported placeOrder handler receives the request from the caller outside this file. Architecture metadata shows it is registered as POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout with auth: none.
The handler takes the target basket identifier directly from the request path.
The basket is looked up solely by the supplied ID, with no user or owner constraint.
The only identity-related operation retrieves the caller's email; it does not reject unauthenticated requests or compare the caller to the basket owner.
After processing the selected basket, the handler destroys all basket items for the supplied BasketId, making the unauthorized checkout destructive.

title: Caller-controlled UserId selects wallets for debit and credit
description: The request body controls UserId, which is used directly to select the wallet that is charged and to select the wallet receiving bonus points. Because the route has no authentication middleware and there is no ownership or authorization check, an attacker can submit another user's UserId to debit that user's wallet or credit arbitrary wallets with bonus points. This is both object-level authorization failure and caller control of a sensitive model property.

trace.description: The exported checkout handler receives externally controlled request data; the route is registered without authentication middleware.
The handler trusts req.body.UserId as the identity for wallet operations rather than deriving the user identity from a verified session.
The supplied UserId selects the wallet whose balance is checked and potentially debited.
The selected user's wallet is decremented based on the checkout total, with no ownership or role check.
The same caller-selected UserId is used to increment bonus points, allowing arbitrary wallet crediting as well.

title: Unsigned client-supplied coupon data grants campaign discounts
description: The fallback coupon flow treats a base64-encoded request field as an authoritative discount credential. Base64 provides no integrity or authenticity protection, so an attacker can construct couponData containing a campaign code and its known validOn timestamp and receive the corresponding discount. The resulting discount is applied to the order total without server-side possession or signature verification.

trace.description: The checkout handler receives request body fields from the external caller.
calculateApplicableDiscount uses the client-supplied couponData whenever the basket does not already contain a coupon.
The value is merely base64-decoded and split; no signature, MAC, server-side token lookup, or other integrity check is performed before extracting the coupon code and date.
A caller-provided campaign code and timestamp are accepted whenever they match a static campaign entry, and the associated discount is returned as valid.
The returned discount is applied directly to totalPrice, reducing the amount recorded and charged for the order.

title: Non-atomic wallet balance check permits concurrent overspending
description: Wallet solvency is checked in one operation and the balance is decremented in a separate operation. Concurrent checkout requests for the same UserId can both observe the same sufficient balance before either decrement occurs, then both decrement it, allowing the wallet to become overdrawn and enabling purchases exceeding the user's funds. No transaction, row lock, or conditional atomic decrement enforces the invariant.

trace.description: The externally reachable checkout handler accepts a request that can initiate wallet payment.
The wallet identity and payment mode are taken from request-controlled fields, so concurrent requests can target the same wallet.
The code first reads the wallet balance and verifies it is at least the order total.
The balance is decremented afterward in a separate database operation, without an atomic balance predicate or transaction tying it to the prior check.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of asset from private directory
description: The unauthenticated privacy-policy proof route serves a file located under the frontend's `assets/private` directory. Because the handler applies no authentication or authorization check before calling `sendFile`, any remote caller can retrieve the supposedly private asset by requesting the registered GET endpoint. The exposed file is an image, so the immediate impact appears limited, but this is an exposed internal resource and could disclose sensitive content if the asset is intended to remain private.

trace.description: The exported handler is registered outside this file as unauthenticated GET `/we/may/also/instruct/you/to/refuse/all/reasonably/necessary/responsibility`; this function receives the attacker-facing request without any visible auth or authorization middleware.
The returned Express callback accepts the request and response but performs no identity, role, or resource-access check before serving the file.
The handler sends `frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/thank-you.jpg` directly to the caller, exposing a resource stored in a directory explicitly named `private` through the unauthenticated route.

title: Authenticated SSRF through profile image URL fetch
description: The profile-image URL endpoint accepts a caller-controlled URL and passes it directly to server-side fetch after only checking that the caller has a valid session. There is no scheme, hostname, IP-range, redirect, or destination allow-list validation. An authenticated attacker can provide targets such as localhost, cloud metadata endpoints, or internal administrative services and cause the server to issue requests from its network position. The response body is then consumed and written to the application's filesystem.

trace.description: POST /profile/image/url invokes the exported middleware; the route caller and its external request data are outside this file. The handler receives the attacker-controlled request body through req.
The handler reads req.body.imageUrl into url. The only security check before use is a session lookup at line 21; that check authenticates the caller but does not constrain the destination URL.
The server performs an outbound request to the caller-supplied url without validating its protocol, hostname, resolved address, redirects, or whether it targets private/internal networks.

title: Unbounded remote response written to local storage
description: A single authenticated request can make the server fetch and persist an arbitrarily large or indefinitely slow response. The handler does not enforce a maximum response size, validate Content-Length, apply a fetch timeout, or otherwise bound the amount of data streamed to disk. Repeated requests can therefore consume filesystem capacity and keep server resources occupied; a large response can also exhaust downstream processing or storage.

trace.description: POST /profile/image/url invokes the exported middleware; the route caller and external request body are outside this file. The handler accepts an imageUrl value from req.body.
The caller-controlled imageUrl is assigned to url and used to initiate a remote fetch. No request-level rate limit, response-size limit, or timeout is implemented in this handler.

The complete response body is converted into a stream and piped into a filesystem write stream. There is no byte counter, maximum-size check, abort timeout, or storage quota enforcement before or during the write.

title: Unbounded profile image upload can exhaust memory and disk
description: The profile image upload handler accepts the entire in-memory uploaded file and writes it to disk without enforcing a size limit, byte-count check, or other per-request resource bound in this file. An attacker can repeatedly submit very large image files: the upload middleware first retains the file in memory (`req.file.buffer`), `file-type` processes the buffer, and `fs.writeFile` persists it under the publicly served uploads directory. If the upstream middleware does not impose a strict limit, this permits memory and disk exhaustion and can degrade or stop service.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported handler is used for POST /profile/image/file; the route and upload middleware are registered outside this file. The caller supplies the multipart file that reaches this handler.

The handler receives the uploaded file from req.file and obtains the complete in-memory buffer. No maximum byte length or file-size validation is performed before the buffer is retained and processed.
The complete attacker-supplied buffer is parsed by file-type, causing processing cost to scale with the uploaded payload without a limit enforced by this handler.
The unbounded buffer is written to the server's uploads directory, consuming disk proportional to the attacker-controlled upload size; repeated requests can exhaust memory and storage.

title: Backslash path traversal allows arbitrary file reads on Windows
description: The file-serving handler attempts to prevent traversal by rejecting only the forward-slash character, but it passes the resulting attacker-controlled value to `path.resolve()` and `res.sendFile()`. On Windows, a parameter such as `..\\..\\sensitive.txt` contains no forward slash, passes line 13, and is resolved outside `ftp/quarantine/` before being served. An attacker can therefore read arbitrary files accessible to the application process by supplying backslash-based parent-directory traversal in `params.file`.

trace.description: The exported handler is invoked by a caller outside this file and receives the attacker-controlled Express request, including `params.file`.
The requested filename is copied directly from the route parameter without canonicalization, platform-independent separator handling, or confinement to the quarantine directory.

The only validation rejects `/`; a Windows backslash traversal value such as `..\\..\\secret.txt` passes this check, is resolved outside the quarantine directory by `path.resolve()`, and is then served to the caller via `res.sendFile()`.

title: Unauthenticated access to recycle records by ID
description: The exported GET handler retrieves a recycle record using the caller-controlled `req.params.id` and returns it without any authentication or per-record authorization check. The route context declares `GET /api/Recycles/:id` with no authentication middleware, so an unauthenticated attacker can request another record by substituting its identifier and receive its serialized contents. This is an unauthenticated object-level authorization failure (BOLA).

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file invokes the exported `getRecycleItem` route handler for `GET /api/Recycles/:id`; the route is registered without authentication middleware.

The handler takes the attacker-controlled path parameter `req.params.id`, parses it, and uses it as the sole record-selection criterion. No authenticated identity or ownership constraint is added to the lookup.
The result of the unrestricted ID lookup is serialized and sent directly to the caller, with no authorization check before disclosure.

title: Unauthenticated triggering of repeat challenge notifications
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/repeat-notification route accepts an arbitrary challenge name and triggers a notification whenever the globally resolved challenge is marked solved. No authenticated identity or authorization check binds the notification to the requesting user, and the route is explicitly registered with no authentication middleware. An attacker can repeatedly request a solved challenge's name and cause notifications to be emitted despite not being authorized to invoke this user-facing action, potentially spamming notification recipients.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives the HTTP request for GET /rest/repeat-notification, a route registered without authentication middleware.
The handler takes the attacker-controlled query parameter challenge and decodes it into challengeName without establishing the caller's identity or ownership of the challenge state.
The supplied name is used to resolve a challenge, and the only condition checked is whether that challenge is marked solved; there is no per-user authorization check.
Even the solved-state gate is only a challenge property check and is not bound to the requesting user.
The handler invokes sendNotification for the selected solved challenge, allowing an unauthenticated caller to trigger the notification side effect.

title: Unauthenticated password-reset security answers are not rate limited
description: The unauthenticated password-reset endpoint performs a security-sensitive database lookup and, on a correct security-answer comparison, changes the account password, but this file contains no rate limiting, attempt counter, lockout, or other abuse control. An attacker can repeatedly submit email/answer combinations to perform unlimited security-question guesses and force repeated database lookups and password-reset processing. Any reverse-proxy or global throttling would need to be verified elsewhere; none is visible in this handler.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives attacker-controlled request data for the unauthenticated POST /rest/user/reset-password route.

The handler accepts the account email and security-question answer directly from the request body and performs no visible rate-limit, retry-count, lockout, token-expiration, or other anti-guessing check before using them as the reset authenticator.

Each request executes a SecurityAnswerModel lookup joined to UserModel by the supplied email, then compares the supplied answer's HMAC with the stored answer; repeated requests can therefore drive unlimited authentication guesses and database work.
A correct guessed answer permits the unauthenticated caller to update the selected user's password, completing the reset.

title: SQL injection in product search query
description: The unauthenticated product-search handler incorporates the caller-controlled `q` query parameter directly into a raw SQL statement using template interpolation. Because the value is not passed as a bound parameter or constrained by an SQL-aware allow-list, an attacker can inject SQL syntax into the `LIKE` predicates, potentially altering query logic or extracting additional database data. The 200-character truncation limits length but does not prevent SQL injection.

trace.description: The exported search handler is registered as the unauthenticated `GET /rest/products/search` route; its caller is outside this file. The handler receives attacker-controlled query data through `req.query.q`.
The `q` value is copied into `criteria` and only length-truncated to 200 characters. No SQL escaping, parameter binding, or structural allow-list is applied.
The untrusted `criteria` value is interpolated into a raw SQL string passed to `models.sequelize.query`, allowing attacker input to alter the SQL expression.

title: Unbounded and potentially expensive product search
description: The public search endpoint executes a potentially expensive database operation with no application-level rate limit, pagination, result cap, or query timeout visible in this handler. `SELECT *` can return every non-deleted product, while caller-controlled leading-wildcard patterns such as `%` can force broad scans and the unconditional `ORDER BY name` adds sorting work. Repeated requests or a broad search can consume database CPU, memory, and response bandwidth.

trace.description: The unauthenticated `GET /rest/products/search` route invokes this handler; the route caller and any infrastructure-level throttling are outside this file.
The attacker controls the search criterion through `req.query.q`; it is capped at 200 characters but wildcard-heavy values remain possible, and there is no pagination or maximum-result parameter.
The handler performs `SELECT *` over all non-deleted products, applies leading-wildcard `LIKE` predicates and sorts the full result by name, then serializes the complete result set with `res.json`.

title: Client-controlled header trusted as login IP
description: The authenticated user's `lastLoginIp` is populated from the caller-controlled `true-client-ip` HTTP header rather than from the server-side socket address or a trusted proxy. Even when the challenge-specific branch is disabled, `sanitizeSecure` appears to sanitize content rather than verify that the value is a legitimate client IP. When `httpHeaderXssChallenge` is enabled, the value bypasses even that sanitization entirely. An authenticated attacker can therefore submit an arbitrary value and have it persisted as their login IP, corrupting security/audit metadata and potentially affecting downstream consumers of this field.

trace.description: The exported route handler receives the attacker-controlled Express request; the caller and route registration are outside this file. The route is GET /rest/saveLoginIp and has no route-level authentication middleware, although the handler performs its own authentication check.

The handler accepts the `true-client-ip` request header as the candidate login IP. This header is supplied by the client unless a trusted proxy is enforced elsewhere, which is not established in this file.

The value is sanitized only when the HTTP-header-XSS challenge is disabled; in the enabled branch no sanitization or IP validation is performed. Even the normal branch does not establish that the value came from a trusted proxy or represents the actual remote address.
The fallback to `req.socket.remoteAddress` occurs only when the header value is undefined, so a caller-provided arbitrary header value normally bypasses the server-derived address.

The attacker-influenced value is persisted to the authenticated user's `lastLoginIp` field. The ORM update prevents this from being a query injection, but it does not protect the integrity of the stored security metadata.

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of security questions by arbitrary email
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/user/security-question endpoint accepts an arbitrary email address and returns the corresponding user's security question. The caller can supply any victim email without proving ownership or completing an authentication step. This discloses a security-recovery factor and also distinguishes existing accounts from unknown addresses via the different `{}` versus question responses, enabling account enumeration and facilitating attacks against any downstream security-question recovery flow.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the Express request from the caller outside this file. It is registered as GET /rest/user/security-question with no authentication middleware, so the request is unauthenticated.
The handler takes the caller-controlled `email` query parameter without requiring an authenticated identity or proof that the caller controls the referenced account.
The attacker-controlled email is used to locate a SecurityAnswer record through an associated User record whose email matches the supplied value. No ownership or authorization check is performed.
The matched answer's SecurityQuestionId is used to retrieve the security question, again without authentication or account-ownership verification.
The security question is returned to the unauthenticated caller. If no matching record exists, the separate empty response at line 25 also permits account existence probing.

title: User-controlled product ID concatenated into MongoDB $where expression
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/products/:id/reviews route receives the path parameter at the exported handler boundary. When the noSqlCommandChallenge feature is enabled, the value is only truncated to 40 characters and is not restricted to a numeric product identifier. It is then concatenated directly into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. An attacker can supply JavaScript syntax in :id, changing the expression executed by MongoDB and potentially performing NoSQL JavaScript injection, including expensive operations or other unauthorized query behavior. The normal Number() branch prevents this only when the challenge is disabled; truncation is not an injection-safe control.

The path parameter is converted to a number only when the noSqlCommandChallenge is disabled. When that challenge is enabled, utils.trunc limits length but does not enforce numeric content or otherwise neutralize JavaScript syntax.
The resulting attacker-influenced id is concatenated into the $where string, producing executable MongoDB JavaScript rather than a bound scalar query value.
MongoDB evaluates the constructed $where expression while finding reviews, providing the injection execution sink.

title: Unbounded product review listing without pagination or result limit
description: The public product-review listing performs a database find and serializes every matching review in one response. There is no pagination, result limit, timeout, or other per-request bound in this handler. A product with a large number of reviews can therefore cause excessive database work, memory use, and response generation for a single request; repeated unauthenticated requests can amplify the impact. The separately identified $where injection can make the work substantially worse when its challenge-enabled branch is active.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; an unauthenticated client can invoke GET /rest/products/:id/reviews through the handler returned by showProductReviews.
The handler issues a find operation for the requested product but does not apply pagination, a maximum result count, or a query timeout.
All retrieved reviews are iterated and then converted into a single JSON response, so database results and response-processing cost scale with the unbounded number of matching reviews.

title: Unauthenticated challenge-progress restoration without user binding
description: The restore-progress endpoint is reachable without authentication and treats any successfully decoded continue code as sufficient authority to mutate challenge state. The handler does not identify the caller, bind the decoded challenge IDs to a user, or verify ownership of the progress being restored. An unauthenticated caller who obtains or generates a valid code can invoke challengeUtils.solve for the selected challenges, affecting the application's challenge state.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler is registered as PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/:continueCode with no authentication middleware and receives the request parameters.
The target progress identifier is taken directly from the unauthenticated route parameter.

Source-controlled credentials can be copied by anyone with repository access and may be reused against the application or other environments. The guidance treats hardcoded credentials as a security misconfiguration even when they appear in a test file.

trace.description: The test invokes the application's login flow using an administrative account; the login implementation is outside this file.
The administrative password admin123 is embedded as a plaintext source literal and passed directly to login.

title: Hardcoded privileged account credentials in test source
description: The test source contains hardcoded authentication credentials for multiple accounts, including the privileged `admin` account with the weak password `admin123` (lines 54-55). Anyone who can read this repository, test artifact, or source bundle can obtain credentials and authenticate as those accounts. Although these may be intended for a test environment, hardcoded credentials in source are unsafe and become a direct account-compromise risk if the accounts or passwords are reused outside isolated tests.

trace.description: The test suite initializes the application and then exercises authenticated deluxe-membership endpoints; the application and account provisioning are outside this file.
The test selects the administrative account and constructs an authenticated request flow using credentials embedded directly in the test source.
The privileged account password `admin123` is hardcoded and passed to `login`, exposing a reusable administrative credential to anyone with access to this source or its artifacts.

title: Hardcoded plaintext user and administrative credentials in source
description: The test source contains plaintext authentication credentials, including the administrative account password `admin123` and multiple user passwords. These values are committed in source and can be disclosed through repository access, logs, artifacts, or accidental deployment. If the corresponding accounts exist outside an isolated test database, an attacker who obtains the source can authenticate directly; the administrative credential presents additional risk. The test-only context reduces confirmed production impact but does not make hardcoded credentials safe.

title: Public directory listing of encryption key files
description: The application exposes a directory listing for `/encryptionkeys` without authentication or authorization. The test explicitly expects a successful HTML directory listing, allowing attackers to enumerate key files and other internal encryption material.

trace.description: The test issues an unauthenticated GET request to `/encryptionkeys`; the caller and route implementation are outside this file, while this file demonstrates the externally reachable entrypoint.
The response is expected to succeed with HTTP 200, showing that no authentication or authorization is required for the directory resource.
The response is expected to be an HTML directory listing whose title is `listing directory /encryptionkeys`, confirming exposure of the directory contents.

title: Public exposure of the premium-content AES key
description: A premium-content AES key is directly retrievable through an unauthenticated GET request to `/encryptionkeys/premium.key`. Disclosure of the key defeats the confidentiality of content protected with it and enables attackers to unlock premium content, as demonstrated by the adjacent premium-content request.

trace.description: The test issues a GET request for `/encryptionkeys/premium.key` without supplying credentials; the caller and route implementation are outside this file.
The test expects the key request to return HTTP 200, demonstrating that the encryption key is publicly retrievable.

The same test suite accesses the premium-content resource through its hidden URL and expects HTTP 200, providing the concrete impact of exposing the key: the protected content can be obtained by an unauthenticated attacker.

title: Public exposure of access log files
description: The application publicly serves an access log file. The test performs an unauthenticated request and expects the log to be returned as an octet-stream, exposing internal logging data and potentially request metadata useful for reconnaissance or incident data leakage.

trace.description: The test issues an unauthenticated GET request for `/support/logs/access.log.<timestamp>`; the caller and serving route are outside this file.
The response is expected to return HTTP 200, showing that the access-log resource is reachable through the application without an authorization check visible at this call site.
The response is expected to have `application/octet-stream` content, confirming that the access log itself is served to the requester rather than denied or restricted.

title: Successful data-erasure request does not erase the account
description: The data-erasure workflow accepts an authenticated erasure request and returns success, but the target account remains usable afterward. The test submits the erasure request, receives HTTP 200, then successfully logs into the same account. This defeats the stated deletion workflow and can leave personal data retained despite an apparent erasure confirmation.

trace.description: The test invokes the POST /dataerasure/ erasure workflow using an authenticated user's token.
The request submits the authenticated user's email as the erasure target and expects a successful HTML response.
The server returns HTTP 200 for the erasure request.
The test then performs a normal login for the supposedly erased account and receives HTTP 200, demonstrating that the account and its data remain active.

title: User-controlled layout path enables arbitrary local file disclosure
description: The POST /dataerasure/ flow accepts a caller-controlled layout path. Supplying ../package.json causes the response to contain package metadata, demonstrating local file disclosure and path traversal through the rendering/layout mechanism. An attacker who can reach this endpoint could substitute other readable filesystem paths, potentially exposing configuration files, source code, or credentials.

trace.description: The test invokes POST /dataerasure/ as an authenticated user; the route handler that processes the request is outside this file.
The request supplies ../package.json as the layout parameter without any visible allow-list or path restriction.
The server returns HTTP 200 and the response includes the package name and truncation marker, proving that the attacker-controlled filesystem path was read and incorporated into the response.

title: Filesystem errors are exposed in the data-erasure response
description: A nonexistent attacker-supplied layout path causes the endpoint to return an internal filesystem error containing the operating-system message 'no such file or directory'. This exposes implementation and filesystem details to the requester and is consistent with verbose/debug error handling being enabled on an externally reachable endpoint.

trace.description: The test invokes POST /dataerasure/ with an authenticated token; the route implementation is outside this file.
The request passes a nonexistent relative filesystem path through the layout parameter.
The endpoint returns HTTP 500 and includes the raw filesystem error text 'no such file or directory' in the response body.

title: Reusable account credentials hardcoded in test source
description: The test source contains reusable account passwords in plaintext, including the password supplied to login calls and the same credential reused in a direct login request. Anyone with access to the repository or test artifacts can use these credentials against any environment where the fixture accounts exist. These may be intentionally seeded test accounts, so exploitability in production is not confirmed from this file alone.

trace.description: Execution of the test suite is the entrypoint; the test runner outside this file causes these literal credentials to be used against the application.
The plaintext password is propagated into the authentication helper and is also repeated in a later direct login request.
The credential is sent to the live application login endpoint, where it authenticates the fixture account.

title: Feedback creation trusts caller-controlled UserId
description: The feedback creation endpoint accepts a caller-supplied `UserId` and persists it without binding the feedback to the authenticated identity or otherwise authorizing attribution to that user. The test demonstrates that an authenticated caller can submit `UserId: 3` and receive a successful response showing the feedback attributed to that account. A separate anonymous test at lines 36-55 demonstrates the same issue without authentication. An attacker can therefore create feedback in another user's name, corrupting attribution and potentially affecting workflows that trust the feedback owner.

trace.description: HTTP POST /api/Feedbacks is exercised as the attacker-facing entrypoint; the route handler is outside this file.

The authenticated request includes an arbitrary `UserId: 3` in the JSON body, while the caller's identity is represented separately by the bearer token. No ownership or authorization value is supplied for changing attribution.
The request succeeds with HTTP 201, demonstrating that the server accepts and processes the caller-controlled user identifier.
The response confirms that the persisted feedback has `UserId` 3, establishing unauthorized attribution to a user selected by the caller.

title: Hardcoded account credential in test source
description: The test source contains a hardcoded reusable account password and passes it directly to the login helper. Because the repository source is available to anyone with access to it, the credential can be recovered and reused against the corresponding application or test deployment if that account exists there. The value is merely base64-looking text, not a protected secret. The exact deployment exposure cannot be confirmed from this test file, so impact is limited to environments sharing this credential.

trace.description: The login test is the entrypoint that initiates authentication using credentials embedded in this source file.
A fixed email address and hardcoded password string are stored directly in the test code and supplied as login input.
The hardcoded credential is passed to the authentication helper, which obtains a bearer token that is then used for authenticated API requests.

title: Public FTP directory listing exposes internal file inventory
description: The test sends an unauthenticated request to GET /ftp and verifies that the application returns an HTML directory listing. Exposing directory indexes allows attackers to enumerate internal files and identify sensitive artifacts such as backups, configuration files, databases, and quarantine contents. No authentication or access restriction is exercised before the listing is served.

trace.description: The test caller, outside this file, invokes the application without credentials through Supertest and requests the FTP root.
The request targets the publicly reachable /ftp resource.
The test confirms a successful HTML directory listing whose title is 'listing directory /ftp', demonstrating that internal file enumeration is enabled.

title: Sensitive confidential and KeePass files are publicly downloadable
description: The application serves sensitive files from the publicly reachable /ftp path without any authentication or authorization in the request. The test explicitly labels acquisitions.md as confidential and confirms it is returned successfully; it also confirms that a KeePass database file is directly downloadable with HTTP 200. An attacker can retrieve confidential planning information and potentially obtain an offline credential database for password cracking or unauthorized access.

trace.description: The test caller, outside this file, requests the confidential acquisitions document through Supertest without supplying credentials.
The request is propagated to the directly addressable /ftp/acquisitions.md file.
The application returns HTTP 200 and the expected confidential document content, confirming exposure.
The test caller then requests the KeePass database file without authentication.
The request targets /ftp/incident-support.kdbx as a directly downloadable resource.
The application returns HTTP 200 for the KeePass database, confirming that the sensitive credential-store artifact is exposed.

title: Permissive wildcard CORS policy is codified by HTTP test
description: The application is explicitly expected to return `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for the root HTTP response. If the same permissive CORS policy applies to authenticated or otherwise sensitive API responses, any website can issue cross-origin requests and read those responses, expanding the attack surface for data exposure. This test confirms the permissive policy but does not establish whether credentials or sensitive data are exposed, so impact is context-dependent.

trace.description: The test sends an HTTP GET request to the application under test; the application receives this attacker-reproducible HTTP request from outside this file.
The test requires the response to include `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, confirming that the application is configured to allow every origin rather than an explicit trusted-origin allowlist.

title: Unauthenticated access to server access logs
description: The test demonstrates that an unauthenticated request can retrieve the server's access log through GET /support/logs/:file. The request does not provide credentials or an authorization token, yet the endpoint returns HTTP 200 and serves the result as an octet-stream. Exposing application logs can disclose request paths, identifiers, errors, and other operational or security-sensitive information, enabling reconnaissance and undermining incident response. This is both a logging-monitoring exposure and a security misconfiguration involving an internal log resource.

trace.description: The test enters the support log retrieval workflow by issuing a GET request without authentication; the route handler is outside this file.
The request targets a predictable access-log filename constructed from the current date.
The test confirms the unauthenticated request succeeds with HTTP 200 and that the response is an octet-stream, demonstrating that a log file is served to the caller.

title: Hardcoded plaintext account credentials in authentication tests
description: The test source embeds multiple plaintext authentication credentials, including the administrative password `admin123` and other account passwords. These values are sent directly to the `/rest/user/login` endpoint and are therefore exposed to anyone with repository access; if the corresponding seeded accounts or credentials are reused outside an isolated test environment, an attacker can authenticate as those users, including the administrator. The same pattern appears for additional accounts at lines 90, 104, 118, 132, and 147.

The plaintext credential is transmitted in the login request and accepted as a valid authentication credential, as shown by the expected HTTP 200 response and returned authentication token.

title: Hardcoded privileged account passwords in test source
description: The test source contains plaintext passwords for multiple named accounts, including the administrator and accountant accounts. These credentials are passed directly to the login helper and are therefore exposed to anyone with access to the repository or test artifacts. If these seeded credentials are reused in any non-test environment, an attacker could authenticate as privileged users. Even if limited to test fixtures, storing reusable passwords in source is an unsafe configuration practice.

title: Unauthenticated product update due to missing function-level access control
description: The product update endpoint accepts an unauthenticated PUT request and successfully modifies an existing product. The test sends no Authorization header, targets a product identifier, and receives HTTP 200 with the attacker-supplied description persisted. Any unauthenticated caller can therefore alter product content, enabling unauthorized data tampering and potentially stored XSS depending on downstream rendering.

The request targets the product identified by tamperingProductId and supplies attacker-controlled product content in the description field without setting authHeader or any other authentication credential.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and the response contains the supplied description, demonstrating that the unauthenticated mutation succeeded.

title: Hardcoded plaintext test credential used for authentication
description: The test suite contains a hardcoded username and plaintext password at line 20 and uses them to obtain an authentication token. If this seeded account or password is shared with a deployed or otherwise reachable environment, anyone who obtains the source can authenticate as that user. The test-only context reduces confidence and likely limits impact to the test environment, but the credential should be supplied through isolated test configuration or a fixture that cannot be reused in production.

The setup invokes the login helper using the hardcoded account email and plaintext password, receiving an authentication token.
The resulting token is placed into an Authorization header and reused for authenticated API requests, making the hardcoded credential part of the authentication path.
The plaintext password literal is embedded directly in source code rather than being supplied through isolated test configuration.

title: Password change does not require the current password
description: The password-change flow is successfully executed with an authenticated token but without supplying or validating the user's current password. Lines 98-102 send only the new and repeated passwords and assert a 200 response. Anyone who obtains a valid session token can therefore change the account password without an additional knowledge-factor check, making session theft substantially more damaging and bypassing reauthentication for a sensitive operation.

trace.description: The test invokes the attacker-facing password-change route; the route implementation is outside this file.
A valid bearer token is obtained and the request supplies only new and repeated password values; no current password is included.
The request is accepted with HTTP 200, demonstrating that the sensitive password-change operation succeeds without current-password verification.

title: Passwords are transmitted in URL query parameters
description: The password-change endpoint is exercised through a GET URL containing the current password and new password values. URL query strings are commonly captured by access logs, reverse proxies, browser history, monitoring systems, and potentially referrer metadata. This exposes authentication secrets outside the request body and creates avoidable credential disclosure risk. The test also demonstrates the same pattern with a missing current password, confirming that password material is part of the GET interface.

trace.description: The test invokes the external password-change HTTP route; the route implementation and its intermediary logging configuration are outside this file.
Plaintext current, new, and repeated passwords are placed directly in the URL query string.
The request is sent to the password-change endpoint with the password-bearing URL, creating a risk that intermediaries or application access logs retain the credentials.

title: Hardcoded account credentials and password-reset answers in source
description: This source file embeds account passwords, password-reset answers, and replacement passwords directly in test requests. The values include credentials for named seeded accounts and the corresponding security-question answers. If the test source, artifacts, recordings, or logs are distributed beyond a strictly isolated test environment, these values can enable account authentication or password resets. Even where they are intentionally fixture values, storing authentication material in source is an unsafe configuration and can lead to accidental reuse or disclosure.

The test sends a named account email together with its security-question answer and a replacement password as request data.
Hardcoded authentication material is present in the source, including the reset answer and new password for the account.

title: Hardcoded reusable authentication credential in test source
description: The test source contains a reusable plaintext/encoded account password and uses it to authenticate as `bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com`. Although the value is Base64-like rather than cryptographically protected, anyone with repository or artifact access can recover and reuse the credential. The same credential is duplicated later in the file, increasing the chance of propagation into other environments if the test account or password is shared with a deployed instance.

title: Plaintext and weak account credentials committed in test source
description: The test source contains plaintext credentials for multiple accounts, including an administrator account (`admin123`), a customer account password, and an accountant password. Anyone with access to this repository or its distributed test artifacts can obtain these credentials and attempt authentication against any environment where the corresponding accounts exist. The administrator password is also weak and may be reused as a default credential. The file does not show isolation of these accounts or sourcing credentials from a secure secret store.

The test invokes the shared login helper with hardcoded account identifiers and plaintext passwords, including the administrator password `admin123`.

The hardcoded credentials are passed to the login helper, which authenticates against the test application and returns a bearer token used for API requests. If these accounts or credentials are available outside an isolated test environment, repository readers can reuse them to obtain authenticated access.

title: Server-side request forgery through profile image URL upload
description: The profile-image URL endpoint accepts a caller-controlled `imageUrl` and is demonstrated using a loopback URL. The test starts a local HTTP server, then submits `http://localhost:<port>/...` to `/profile/image/url`; the application successfully processes the response and writes the image file. This establishes server-side fetching of an attacker-selected destination without evidence of an allow-list or private-network restriction. An attacker could target localhost services, cloud instance metadata endpoints, or other internal HTTP services from the application host.

trace.description: The attacker-facing POST `/profile/image/url` route is exercised here; its production handler is outside this file. The request receives external input through the `imageUrl` form field.
The test submits a caller-controlled URL, including a URL pointing to `localhost` and a dynamically selected local port.

The test's local HTTP server is reached by the application and its image response is accepted: the request succeeds and the resulting profile image is written under the user's upload path. The outbound fetch sink is implemented by the route handler outside this file, but this test demonstrates that attacker-selected loopback destinations are processed.

title: Unauthenticated access to recycle records
description: The test exercises GET /api/Recycles/1 without sending an Authorization header and expects a successful response containing recycle records, including UserId and AddressId fields. If this test reflects the deployed route behavior, an unauthenticated caller can retrieve a recycle resource by identifier without authentication or ownership validation. An attacker could enumerate recycle IDs and disclose other users' recycling activity and address references.

trace.description: The attacker-facing route handler is outside this file; this test invokes the GET /api/Recycles/:id endpoint as an unauthenticated caller.
The request targets the caller-supplied resource identifier 1 and does not set authHeader, unlike the POST, PUT, and DELETE requests in this file.

The test asserts HTTP 200 and consumes the returned data, demonstrating that the route is expected to serve the requested resource without an authentication or per-resource authorization check visible in this flow.
The returned records expose ownership and address identifiers through UserId and AddressId, increasing the impact of unauthorized resource access.

title: Empty product search returns an unbounded product collection
description: The tests explicitly establish that the product-search endpoint returns the complete product collection when the query is empty or omitted. A caller can therefore request an unbounded list with a single GET request, and the endpoint's response size and backend work scale with the total catalog rather than a caller-supplied page size. The route implementation is outside this file, so pagination, maximum-result limits, and infrastructure rate limiting cannot be confirmed here; however, these tests document the absence of a bounded search behavior. As the catalog grows, repeated requests or a large catalog can consume application memory, database resources, and response bandwidth.

trace.description: The test invokes the attacker-facing product search request with an empty search parameter; the route handler is outside this file.
The request is sent to GET /rest/products/search?q= with no pagination or result-limit parameter.
The test requires the response to contain as many products as the complete /api/Products collection, confirming that an empty search returns the entire result set.

title: Verbose error responses disclose Express and implementation details
description: The externally reachable GET /redirect route returns a verbose HTML error response when the required query parameter is absent. The response exposes the application name, Express/framework identification, TypeError details, and implementation-specific text such as “of undefined” and “includes”. An unauthenticated attacker can trigger this with a request to /redirect and use the leaked internals to fingerprint the stack and improve subsequent attacks.

The endpoint returns HTTP 500 for malformed attacker-controlled input, demonstrating that the error path is externally reachable.

The response is HTML containing the application name, Express identifier, TypeError text, undefined-property details, and the internal method name 'includes', exposing framework and implementation information to unauthenticated callers.

title: Malformed redirect requests expose detailed framework errors
description: The same publicly reachable /redirect error path leaks internal exception details when an unrecognized query parameter is supplied. A request containing ?x=y produces a 500 response whose HTML identifies Express and reveals TypeError/undefined/includes implementation details. This provides unauthenticated technology and failure-mode disclosure and indicates production-style error handling is enabled on the route.

The malformed request reaches an unhandled error path and returns HTTP 500.
The HTML error response exposes the application name, Express, TypeError, undefined-property information, and the internal 'includes' method name.

title: Redirect allowlist can be bypassed through embedded allowed URLs
description: Redirect target validation appears to accept a target because an allow-listed URL is merely embedded in its query string: /score-board?satisfyIndexOf=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop. This demonstrates substring/containment-based validation rather than exact validation of the redirect destination. If the handler applies the same check to attacker-supplied absolute URLs containing an allowed string, an attacker could construct an external redirect target and abuse the endpoint for phishing or trust-boundary bypasses. The test confirms the weak validation shape but does not, by itself, demonstrate an external attacker-controlled host, so confidence is moderate.

trace.description: The test supplies attacker-controlled data in the GET /redirect 'to' query parameter; the route handler is outside this file.

The supplied destination embeds an allow-listed GitHub URL inside the query string of a different path, indicating that validation is based on finding an allowed substring within the full target rather than validating the destination origin/path as a structured URL.
The route accepts the crafted target and follows one redirect successfully, confirming that the embedded allow-listed value is sufficient for redirect acceptance.

title: Unauthenticated security-question disclosure and account enumeration
description: The security-question endpoint is exercised without authentication and returns a user's security question when supplied only with the user's email address. An attacker who knows or guesses an email address can retrieve the first factor used by the password-recovery workflow, and the distinct empty response for unknown addresses also enables account enumeration. The test does not show the subsequent reset operation, so the full account-takeover impact cannot be confirmed from this file alone.

trace.description: The test invokes GET /rest/user/security-question without an Authorization header; the route handler is outside this file and receives the request externally.
The caller supplies an email address as the sole lookup input in the query string, with no visible authentication or authorization context.
The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and exposes the matching user's security-question text, demonstrating that possession of an email address is sufficient to retrieve this security-recovery information.

title: Verbose ORM error details exposed for missing email parameter
description: A request omitting the required email parameter produces an HTTP 500 response containing HTML with the application name and the underlying ORM error, including the invalid undefined WHERE value. This exposes internal implementation details to an unauthenticated caller and indicates that malformed input is not converted into a controlled client error.

The request reaches the endpoint with the email value absent, causing the backend lookup to receive an undefined parameter.

The endpoint returns HTTP 500 HTML containing the application name and the database/ORM error text `WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value`, confirming verbose internal error disclosure.

title: Order tracking can trigger an unbounded collection-wide response
description: The test demonstrates that the order-tracking endpoint accepts an attacker-controlled orderId expression and returns an array containing every matching order rather than a bounded single-order result. Because the response is unpaginated and the injected value causes a collection-wide query, a caller can make one request materialize and serialize the entire order dataset, with memory, database, and response-bandwidth costs scaling with the number of stored orders. This file is a test rather than the route implementation, so the underlying reachability and any infrastructure-level limits cannot be confirmed here.

The request supplies a crafted orderId value containing a boolean expression, demonstrating that caller-controlled input is accepted by the tracking operation.

The test requires a successful JSON response whose data field is an array and iterates over every returned order, establishing that the crafted request can produce a collection-wide response rather than a bounded single-order result.

title: Security-answer creation trusts a caller-supplied user identifier
description: The test authenticates with a pre-existing bearer token and then submits a client-controlled `UserId` when creating a security answer. The request is expected to succeed with HTTP 201, indicating that the API may permit an authenticated caller to create a security answer for an arbitrary user identifier rather than binding the answer to the authenticated user. If the target user has not yet created an answer, an attacker could potentially populate that user's security-answer record and interfere with account-recovery or verification workflows. The route implementation is outside this file, so ownership enforcement cannot be confirmed here.

title: Hardcoded test account password in source
description: The test setup embeds a reusable account password directly in source code and uses it to authenticate as `jim@juice-sh.op`. If this credential corresponds to a deployed or shared account, anyone with repository or artifact access can recover and replay it, potentially gaining authenticated access. Although this appears to be a test fixture, hardcoded credentials should be replaced with isolated test configuration or generated test users.

title: Unauthenticated caller can create an administrator account via role mass assignment
description: The public POST /api/Users endpoint accepts a caller-supplied `role` property and persists `role: 'admin'` without authentication or server-side privilege authorization. An unauthenticated attacker can create an administrator account by submitting the same request, gaining elevated application privileges. This is both a sensitive-property mass-assignment issue and a function-level access-control failure.

title: User-controlled fields parameter exposes password data
description: The `/rest/user/whoami` endpoint allows an authenticated user to control a `fields` query parameter and returns the password property when `password` is requested. The test confirms the response contains a string password value. This exposes password material, likely a stored hash, to the account holder and defeats the intended property-level restriction that omits passwords by default.

Anyone who can read the repository or test artifacts can obtain these credentials and attempt to authenticate as the administrator. If this account or password is shared with any deployed, staging, or otherwise reachable environment, the attacker may gain administrative access. Even if intended only for a test environment, embedding a real administrative credential in source is an unsafe secret-management configuration.

title: Unauthenticated chat can generate unrestricted discount coupons
description: The unauthenticated POST /rest/chat handler exposes the generateCoupon tool. Although the system prompt states that coupons require a verified damaged order, explicit return rejection, and a maximum 10% discount, the tool implementation performs no authentication, order verification, return-status verification, or server-side discount bound. Any caller can submit a chat request designed to cause the model to invoke generateCoupon, and the tool will generate a coupon for an arbitrary numeric discount, including values above 10%. This is both a broken function-level authorization boundary and excessive agency because a model decision directly triggers a privileged coupon-generation operation without independently enforcing the caller's authorization or business-policy conditions.

The handler reads caller-controlled chat messages and passes them into the LLM invocation, allowing an unauthenticated caller to request or influence tool use.
The LLM is given generateCoupon as an executable tool, so model output can trigger coupon generation as part of the chat request.

The generateCoupon tool accepts only a numeric discount and directly calls security.generateCoupon. There is no user authentication check, order lookup, damaged-order validation, return/rejection validation, or maximum-discount enforcement before the coupon is created.

title: Unauthenticated chat accepts unbounded LLM input without application-level throttling
description: The request body contains an unbounded messages array and is sent directly to the LLM. This route has no visible per-user/IP rate limit, message-count limit, token/input-size limit, timeout, or request-level cost control. A caller can repeatedly submit very large message histories, causing proportionally expensive LLM input processing and streaming work. The tool loop is capped at 10 steps, but that does not bound the size of the initial messages or the number of requests an unauthenticated caller can make.

The unbounded messages value is passed directly to streamText, which invokes the configured external LLM and streams a response. Only tool steps are capped at 10; the input size, request frequency, and LLM processing cost are not bounded here.

title: User-controlled username is injected into the LLM system prompt
description: A username retrieved from the authenticated token's user record is interpolated directly into the LLM system prompt without fencing or escaping. If a user can choose a username containing instruction-like text, that text is placed in the system/instruction channel rather than ordinary user-message content and can alter the model's interpretation of the prompt. In combination with executable tools, this can encourage unintended tool calls. The ability to set or modify usernames is outside this file, so confidence is lower, but the unsafe system-prompt construction is visible here.

The resulting string is supplied as the LLM system prompt while executable tools are enabled, allowing injected username text to influence model tool-selection behavior.

title: Generated REST collections have pagination disabled
description: The application enables Finale-generated CRUD endpoints for every listed model with `pagination: false`. Public or merely authenticated collection endpoints can therefore return the entire table in one response, with result size and database work growing with the number of records. An attacker can repeatedly request unbounded collections such as `/api/Products`, `/api/Feedbacks`, or other generated list endpoints to consume database, memory, CPU, and response bandwidth.

title: Generated CRUD endpoints use implicit field exposure and mass assignment
description: The Finale REST layer is configured with `excludeAttributes` rather than an explicit writable/readable allow-list. Most models, including User, Product, Feedback, BasketItem, Complaint, Card, Quantity, and Hint, have an empty exclusion list; User excludes only `password` and `totpSecret`. Consequently, generated create/update/read operations can bind or expose every other model property. If a model contains privilege, ownership, pricing, status, or other internal fields, callers can set or retrieve those fields without field-level authorization. The same configuration also makes newly added sensitive model fields automatically exposed.

title: Password-reset rate limiting trusts attacker-controlled proxy identity
description: The reset-password rate limiter derives its bucket key from the proxy-derived client IP while the application globally enables `trust proxy`. When the application is directly reachable or the proxy trust boundary is misapplied, an attacker can supply or manipulate `X-Forwarded-For` values so requests are assigned to different buckets. This permits effectively unbounded reset-password attempts and can consume reset-processing, email, database, or other downstream resources despite the apparent limiter.
